stem: A binary heap is stored in a 0-indexed array. Which expression gives the index of the parent of the node at index `i` (for `i > 0`)?

options.text: `i // 2`, as in a 1-indexed heap
options.why: That is the parent formula for a 1-indexed heap; with 0-indexing it is off by one for every left child.
Children of `p` sit at `2p + 1` and `2p + 2`, so subtracting 1 and halving recovers `p` for both.
For `i = 1` this gives 1, pointing a node at itself instead of at the root.
That is the left child of `i`, not its parent.

explanation: In a 0-indexed array heap the children of index `p` are `2p + 1` and `2p + 2`. Inverting gives `parent(i) = (i - 1) // 2`. For example, index 5 has parent 2, and index 2 has children 5 and 6. The `i // 2` form belongs to 1-indexed heaps, where children are `2p` and `2p + 1`.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: The underlying array of a valid binary min-heap is always sorted in ascending order.

options.text: True
options.why: The heap property only orders each parent against its children, not siblings or cousins.

options.text: False
options.why: `[1, 3, 2]` is a valid min-heap but is not sorted; only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum.

explanation: A heap is partially ordered: every parent is ≤ its children, but nothing constrains siblings. `[1, 3, 2]` and `[1, 2, 3]` are both valid min-heaps. A sorted array is always a valid min-heap, but not the reverse. That's why a heap gives O(1) access to the minimum yet can't be scanned in order without popping.
reference: Python docs: heapq — Heap queue algorithm

stem: Python's `heapq` module only implements a min-heap. What is the usual way to use it as a max-heap of integers?

options.text: Call `heapq.heapify(nums, reverse=True)`
options.why: `heapify` takes no `reverse` argument; passing one raises a TypeError.

options.text: Read the maximum from `heap[-1]`, the last slot
options.why: The last slot is just some leaf; the maximum can be any leaf, not necessarily the last one.

options.text: Push `-x` and negate the value again when you pop
options.why: Negating flips the ordering, so the smallest stored value is the largest original.

options.text: Sort the list in reverse first, then call `heapify`
options.why: `heapify` rearranges the list back into min-heap order, undoing the reverse sort.

explanation: Store negated keys: `heappush(h, -x)` and `-heappop(h)`. For non-numeric items, wrap them in a class with a reversed `__lt__`. Python 3.14 added public max-heap functions (`heapify_max`, `heappush_max`, …), but negation works on every version and is what interviewers expect.
reference: Python docs: heapq — Heap queue algorithm

stem: What is the time complexity of reading (not removing) the minimum element of a binary min-heap with n elements? Answer in Big-O notation.
explanation: The minimum always sits at the root, index 0, so peeking is `heap[0]`: O(1). Removing it costs O(log n), because the last element moves to the root and sifts down one level at a time.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: Match each binary-heap operation with its time complexity for a heap of n elements.

options.text: O(log n)
O(n)

prompts.text: Build a heap from an unsorted array with heapify
Check whether an arbitrary value is in the heap

explanation: Peek reads the root. Insert and remove each walk one root-to-leaf path, which is O(log n) long. Bottom-up heapify is O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a short way. Searching for an arbitrary value has no ordering to exploit, so it scans the array in O(n).
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: What problem is a disjoint-set (union-find) structure designed to answer efficiently?

options.text: Finding the shortest path between two vertices
options.why: That needs BFS or Dijkstra; union-find only tracks which group each element belongs to.

options.text: Whether two items share a group as groups merge
options.why: Its two operations, `union` and `find`, answer dynamic connectivity in near-constant time.

options.text: Keeping a collection sorted under insertions and deletions
options.why: That's the job of a balanced BST or skip list; union-find keeps no order.

options.text: Splitting one group into two groups when an edge is removed
options.why: Standard union-find supports merging only; un-merging needs other structures.

explanation: Union-find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets. `union(a, b)` merges the sets containing a and b, and `find(x)` returns the representative (root) of x's set, so `find(a) == find(b)` tests connectivity. With path compression and union by rank or size, a sequence of m operations costs O(m α(n)). It powers Kruskal's MST, cycle detection in undirected graphs and counting connected components.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 21: Data Structures for Disjoint Sets

stem: Which statements about a standard Bloom filter are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It can say an item might be present when it never was added
options.why: Other items may have set all of its bit positions, giving a false positive.

options.text: If it says an item is absent, the item was definitely never added
options.why: Adding an item sets all of its bits, so any zero bit proves it was never added.

options.text: Items can be removed by clearing their bits
options.why: Bits are shared between items, so clearing them can erase other items and cause false negatives.

options.text: It stores the items so they can be listed later
options.why: It stores only hashed bit positions; the original items can't be recovered.

options.text: It reports exactly how many times an item was added
options.why: A plain Bloom filter is a set-membership test; counting needs a count-min sketch or counters.

explanation: A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions. Adding sets k bits; querying checks those k bits. That gives no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate, using very little memory. Deletion is unsafe in the plain version because bits are shared; a counting Bloom filter replaces bits with small counters to allow removals.
reference: Bloom (1970), Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding

What does this code print?

```python
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print(h)
```

options.why: A heap is not fully sorted; pushes only sift each value up as far as needed.
Tracing each push and sift-up gives exactly this layout.

options.text: `[5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2]`, since pushing keeps insertion order
options.why: Each push sifts the new value up, so the insertion order isn't preserved.
2 can't stay at index 5 under its parent 8 at index 2; it sifts up to index 2.

explanation: Trace: push 5 → [5]. Push 3 → swap with 5 → [3, 5]. Push 8 → [3, 5, 8]. Push 1 → index 3, parent 5 swaps, then parent 3 swaps → [1, 3, 8, 5]. Push 9 → [1, 3, 8, 5, 9]. Push 2 → index 5, parent 8 at index 2 swaps, then parent 1 stops it → [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. Only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum.
reference: Python docs: heapq.heappush

stem:
What does this code print?

```python
import heapq
a = [4, 3, 2, 1]
heapq.heapify(a)
print(a)
```

options.why: That is what four `heappush` calls of 4, 3, 2, 1 produce; bottom-up heapify ends differently.
Heapify sifts down from the last parent; 3 swaps with 1, then 4 sifts down past 1 and 3.

options.text: `[4, 3, 2, 1]`, because heapify returns a new heap
options.why: heapify works in place and returns None; the list itself is rearranged into heap order.
4 at index 1 would be larger than its child 3, which breaks the heap property.

explanation: `heapify` works bottom-up: for each parent from the last one down to the root, sift it down. Index 1 (value 3) swaps with its child 1 → [4, 1, 2, 3]. Index 0 (value 4) swaps with the smaller child 1, then with 3 → [1, 3, 2, 4]. Pushing 4, 3, 2, 1 one at a time instead gives [1, 2, 3, 4]: different procedures can produce different valid heaps.
reference: Python docs: heapq.heapify

stem:
What does this code print?

```python
import heapq
h1 = [1, 3, 5]
h2 = [1, 3, 5]
print(heapq.heappushpop(h1, 0), heapq.heapreplace(h2, 0), h1, h2)
```

options.why: `heappushpop` pushes first, so the new 0 is the smallest and comes straight back out.

options.text: `0 0 [1, 3, 5] [1, 3, 5]`, as both reject a smaller value
options.why: `heapreplace` pops first, returning the old minimum 1 before inserting 0.
Push-then-pop returns 0 unchanged; pop-then-push returns 1 and keeps 0.
This swaps the two functions' semantics.

explanation: `heappushpop(h, x)` behaves like push then pop: when x is smaller than the root, x itself is returned and the heap is untouched. `heapreplace(h, x)` behaves like pop then push: it always returns the old root and always keeps x, even when x is smaller. Both cost one sift, faster than a separate push and pop.
reference: Python docs: heapq.heappushpop, heapq.heapreplace

stem:
This priority queue crashes. Which change fixes it while keeping equal-priority tasks in insertion order?

```python
import heapq
q = []
heapq.heappush(q, (1, {'job': 'a'}))
heapq.heappush(q, (1, {'job': 'b'}))  # TypeError
```

options.text: Push `(1, str(task))` so tied payloads compare as plain strings
options.why: This avoids the crash but orders ties alphabetically, not by insertion, and loses the dict.

options.text: Add `next(counter)` from `itertools.count()` as the middle field
options.why: The unique, increasing counter breaks every tie, so dicts are never compared and FIFO order holds.

options.text: Use `heapq.heappush(q, (1, task), key=lambda t: t[0])`
options.why: `heappush` has no `key` parameter; passing one raises TypeError.

options.text: Wrap the payloads in a list instead, as in `(1, [task])`
options.why: Python would then compare the lists, which compare the dicts inside them and still fail.

explanation: Tuples compare element by element. When priorities tie, Python compares the next field, and `dict < dict` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict'`. A monotonically increasing counter as the second field is unique, so comparison never reaches the payload, and earlier insertions win ties. The heapq docs recommend exactly this pattern.
reference: Python docs: heapq — Priority Queue Implementation Notes

stem:
What does `kth([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2)` return? Type the number.

```python
import heapq
def kth(nums, k):
    h = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k:
            heapq.heappop(h)
    return h[0]
```
explanation: The function keeps a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. Whenever it grows past k, the smallest is popped. At the end the heap holds {5, 6}, and its root, 5, is the 2nd largest. This runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) space, and it also works on a stream.
reference: LeetCode 215: Kth Largest Element in an Array

stem: You keep a min-heap capped at k elements while scanning n numbers to find the k largest. What is the total time complexity?

options.text: O(n log n)
options.why: That would be true if the heap could grow to n elements; capping it at k makes each operation cheaper.

options.text: O(n log k)
options.why: Each of the n elements causes at most a push and a pop on a heap of size k.

options.text: O(k log n), since only k items are ever kept
options.why: The scan touches all n elements, so the cost can't be independent of n's linear factor.

options.text: O(n + k)
options.why: Heap operations aren't constant time; each costs O(log k).

explanation: Every element is pushed once and possibly popped once, each costing O(log k) on a heap of at most k + 1 elements, so the total is O(n log k) time with O(k) extra space. When k is much smaller than n this beats sorting's O(n log n), and unlike sorting it works on a stream that doesn't fit in memory.
reference: Python docs: heapq.nlargest

stem: Which statements about union-find optimisations are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Path compression points nodes on the find path closer to the root
options.why: Later finds on those nodes then take one or two hops instead of walking the whole chain.

options.text: Union by rank or size attaches the shorter tree under the taller one
options.why: This keeps trees shallow; on its own it bounds the height at O(log n).

options.text: With both optimisations, every single find is guaranteed O(1)
options.why: The bound is amortised O(α(n)) per operation; one find can still walk a longer path.

options.text: Path compression makes union by rank unnecessary for any bound
options.why: Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortised; you need both for the α(n) bound.

options.text: These optimisations let union-find split sets apart again
options.why: They only speed up merges and finds; splitting sets is still unsupported.

explanation: Union by rank or size keeps trees balanced, so heights are at most log n. Path compression flattens the paths that finds walk along. Together, m operations on n elements take O(m α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any practical n. That is effectively constant amortised time, not a worst-case O(1) per call.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 21: Data Structures for Disjoint Sets

stem: Put the steps of extracting the minimum from an array-based binary min-heap in order.

options.text: Save the root value as the result
Move the last element of the array into the root slot
Shrink the array by one
Sift the new root down, swapping with its smaller child until the heap property holds
Return the saved value

explanation: Removing the root would leave a hole, so the last leaf fills it. This keeps the tree complete, but the leaf is usually too large for the top, so it sifts down, swapping with the smaller child each time, which takes O(log n). Swapping with the larger child instead would put a too-large value above its sibling and break the heap.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: You merge k sorted lists containing N elements in total by keeping one candidate from each list in a min-heap. What is the time complexity?

options.text: O(N log N), as if every element were sorted together
options.why: The heap never holds more than k items, so each operation costs log k, not log N.

options.text: O(N k)
options.why: That is the cost of scanning all k list heads for the minimum on every step, which the heap avoids.

options.text: O(N log k)
options.why: Each of the N elements is pushed and popped once on a heap of size at most k.

options.text: O(k log N)
options.why: Every one of the N elements has to be output, so the cost is at least linear in N.

explanation: Seed the heap with the head of each list. Then repeatedly pop the smallest, output it, and push the next element from the same list. The heap holds at most k entries, so there are N pops and N pushes at O(log k) each. Python's `heapq.merge` does this lazily and returns an iterator.
reference: Python docs: heapq.merge

stem: An LRU cache must support `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` in O(1), evicting the least recently used entry when full. Which design achieves this?

options.text: A min-heap keyed by last-access time
options.why: Updating an entry's time on every access needs a decrease-key, which costs O(log n), not O(1).

options.text: A hash map of keys to nodes in a doubly linked list
options.why: The map finds a node in O(1), and the list moves or removes it in O(1) with prev/next pointers.

options.text: A hash map plus a Python list of keys in recency order
options.why: Moving a key to the end of a list means removing it from the middle, which is O(n).

options.text: A singly linked list on its own, scanned on each access
options.why: Finding a key means walking the list, which is O(n) per call.

explanation: The classic design pairs a dict for lookup with a doubly linked list for order. On access, unlink the node and move it to the head. On insert into a full cache, drop the tail node and delete its key from the dict. Both pointers are needed so a node can unlink itself in O(1). In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` provides the same behaviour.
reference: LeetCode 146: LRU Cache

stem: Python's `heapq` module provides a decrease-key operation for changing the priority of an item already in the heap.

options.text: True
options.why: No such function exists; heapq only offers push, pop, pushpop, replace, heapify, merge and nlargest/nsmallest.

options.text: False
options.why: You push a new entry with the new priority and skip stale entries when they are popped (lazy deletion).

explanation: heapq has no way to locate or update an existing entry. The standard workaround is lazy deletion. Push the item again with its new priority, and either record the latest priority in a dict or mark the old entry removed. When a popped entry no longer matches, skip it. Dijkstra's algorithm in Python usually does this with an `if d > dist[u]: continue` check. The cost is a heap that can grow to the total number of pushes.
reference: Python docs: heapq — Priority Queue Implementation Notes

stem:
What does this code print?

```python
import heapq
h = [2, 7, 4, 9]
heapq.heappop(h)
print(h)
```

options.text: `[7, 4, 9]`, the remaining items in their old order
options.why: That just deletes the first slot; the heap must then be repaired, putting the smallest value at the root.
9 moves to the root, then swaps with its smaller child 4.
9 swaps with the smaller child 4 at index 2, so it ends at index 2 and 7 stays at index 1.
7 at the root is larger than its child 4, which breaks the heap property.

explanation: Pop removes 2 and moves the last element, 9, to the root: [9, 7, 4]. Sifting down compares 9 with its children 7 and 4 and swaps with the smaller, 4, giving [4, 7, 9]. Swapping with the smaller child is what keeps the heap valid.
reference: Python docs: heapq.heappop

stem: Bottom-up `heapify` on n elements runs in O(n), even though sift-down can cost O(log n). Why?

options.text: Most elements are already in place, so they need no sifting
options.why: The input can be in reverse order; the bound holds for any input, not just nearly-sorted ones.

options.text: Most nodes are near the bottom, where sifting down is cheap
options.why: Summing node count × height over all levels gives n·Σh/2^h, which converges to 2n.

options.text: Heapify compares each element only with its parent
options.why: Sift-down compares against children and can descend several levels; the saving comes from where nodes sit.

options.text: The real cost is O(n log n); O(n) is only the average
options.why: The O(n) bound is a worst-case result, not an average.

explanation: Heapify sifts down from the last parent to the root. A node at height h costs O(h), and there are about n/2^(h+1) such nodes. The total is Σ h·n/2^(h+1) = (n/2)·Σ h/2^h = (n/2)·2 = n, which is O(n). Repeated `heappush` is O(n log n) in the worst case, because new values can sift up from deep leaves.
reference: CLRS, Section 6.3: Building a heap

stem:
What does this running-median function return for `[5, 15, 1, 3]`?

```python
import heapq
def medians(stream):
    lo, hi, out = [], [], []   # lo is a max-heap (negated), hi a min-heap
    for x in stream:
        heapq.heappush(lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))
        if len(hi) > len(lo):
            heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))
        out.append(-lo[0] if len(lo) > len(hi) else (-lo[0] + hi[0]) / 2)
    return out
```

options.why: After 3 arrives the values are {1, 3, 5, 15}, so the median is the mean of 3 and 5.

options.text: `[5, 15, 5, 4.0]`, reporting 15 for the pair
options.why: With two elements the code averages both heap tops, giving 10.0.
After 1 arrives the sorted values are [1, 5, 15], whose median is 5.

explanation: Every value passes through `lo` into `hi`, so `hi` always receives the largest of the current lower half. Rebalancing keeps `len(lo)` equal to `len(hi)` or one more. The median is the top of `lo` for an odd count, or the mean of both tops for an even count. Each step is O(log n), and the code gives 5, (5+15)/2 = 10.0, 5, and (3+5)/2 = 4.0.
reference: LeetCode 295: Find Median from Data Stream

stem:
What does this union-find code print?

```python
n = 4
p = list(range(n))
def find(x):
    while p[x] != x:
        x = p[x]
    return x
for a, b in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]:
    p[find(a)] = find(b)
print(p)
```

options.text: `[3, 3, 3, 3]`, with every node pointing at the root
options.why: That would need path compression; this `find` never rewrites parents along the path.
Each union links the current root to the next element's root, building a chain 0→1→2→3.
Roots are linked under `find(b)`, not `find(a)`, so 3 ends up as the root.
union(1, 2) sets the parent of root 1 to 2, so `p[1]` becomes 2.

explanation: union(0, 1) sets p[0] = 1. union(1, 2): find(1) is 1 and find(2) is 2, so p[1] = 2. union(2, 3) sets p[2] = 3. The result is the chain [1, 2, 3, 3]. Without union by rank or size and without path compression, these unions build an n-long chain, so a later find(0) takes O(n). That worst case is what the two optimisations prevent.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 21: Data Structures for Disjoint Sets

stem:
The parent array is the chain `p = [1, 2, 3, 4, 4]` (0→1→2→3→4). What is `p` after one call to this `find(0)`?

```python
def find(x):
    if p[x] != x:
        p[x] = find(p[x])
    return p[x]
```

options.why: This `find` assigns the result back into `p[x]`, so the parents change.
The recursion rewrites every node on the path, not just the starting one.
Each node on the path gets the root as its parent while the recursion unwinds.

options.text: `[0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`, making 0 the new root
options.why: Path compression points nodes at the existing root, 4; it never changes which node is the root.

explanation: This is full path compression. The recursion walks 0→1→2→3→4, finds root 4, and on the way back sets p[3], p[2], p[1] and p[0] to 4. The tree becomes flat, so every later find on these nodes takes one hop. Path halving (`p[x] = p[p[x]]` in a loop) is an iterative alternative with the same amortised bound.
reference: CLRS, Section 21.3: Disjoint-set forests

stem: You need the k-th largest of n numbers. Which statements comparing quickselect with a size-k min-heap are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Quickselect averages O(n) but can degrade to O(n²) with bad pivots
options.why: Each round discards about half the data on average; adversarial pivots discard only one element.

options.text: The heap approach suits a stream of unknown length that won't fit in memory
options.why: It keeps only k values and processes each number once as it arrives.

options.text: The heap approach has a worse worst case than quickselect
options.why: The heap is O(n log k) even in the worst case, which beats quickselect's O(n²) worst case.

options.text: Quickselect leaves the input array unchanged
options.why: Quickselect partitions in place, reordering the array, unless you copy it first.

options.text: Both approaches need O(n) extra memory
options.why: The heap needs only O(k) extra; in-place quickselect needs O(1) beyond its recursion.

explanation: Quickselect partitions around a pivot and recurses into one side: O(n) on average, O(n²) worst case, and median-of-medians guarantees O(n) at a large constant. It needs the whole array in memory and reorders it. A size-k min-heap costs O(n log k) in every case, O(k) memory, and works on streams. When k is small or data streams in, the heap is often the practical choice.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 9: Medians and Order Statistics

options.text: `None`, because no edge revisits a vertex
options.why: Edges 1-2, 2-3 and 3-1 form a triangle, so a cycle exists.
Before edge (2, 3), vertices 2 and 3 are in different sets, so it is just a union.
After the first three edges, 1 and 3 already share a root, so (3, 1) closes the cycle.
The first edge always merges two singleton sets and can never close a cycle.

explanation: For an undirected graph, an edge whose endpoints already share a root connects two vertices that are already connected, so it closes a cycle. The first three edges merge {0, 1, 2, 3} into one set. Then edge (3, 1) finds equal roots and is returned. The `p[x] = p[p[x]]` line is path halving. This check only works for undirected graphs; directed cycles need DFS colouring or topological sort.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 21: Data Structures for Disjoint Sets

stem: A graph has 7 vertices (0–6) and the edges `(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 5), (2, 0)`. Using union-find, how many connected components are there? Type a number.
explanation: Start with 7 components and subtract one for each union that merges two different sets. (0, 1) → 6. (1, 2) → 5. (3, 4) → 4. (5, 5) is a self-loop with the same root, so no change. (2, 0) joins vertices already in the same set, so no change. The components are {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5} and {6}: 4 in total. Vertex 6 has no edges, so it is its own component.
reference: LeetCode 323: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

stem:
What does this print?

```python
import heapq, itertools
c = itertools.count()
q = []
for p, t in [(2, 'b'), (1, 'x'), (2, 'a')]:
    heapq.heappush(q, (p, next(c), t))
print([heapq.heappop(q)[2] for _ in range(3)])
```

options.text: `['x', 'a', 'b']`, ordering ties by task name
options.why: That is what plain `(priority, task)` tuples give, comparing the strings on ties.
Priority 1 comes first; between the two priority-2 tasks, the earlier counter 0 beats 2.
This is insertion order; the heap pops by priority first, so 'x' with priority 1 comes out first.
A min-heap pops the smallest priority first, so 1 comes before 2.

explanation: Tuples compare field by field. 'x' has priority 1, so it pops first. The two priority-2 entries tie on the first field, so the counter decides: 'b' got 0 and 'a' got 2, so 'b' pops before 'a'. The counter gives stable, first-in-first-out ordering among equal priorities and never compares the payloads. Without it, ties fall back to comparing the strings, giving ['x', 'a', 'b'].
reference: Python docs: heapq — Priority Queue Implementation Notes

stem: Match each requirement with the data structure that best fits it.

options.text: Two heaps (a max-heap and a min-heap)
Union-find
Bloom filter
Skip list

prompts.text: Report the median after each number in a stream
Merge friend groups and ask whether two users are connected
Check whether a URL was already crawled using very little memory, tolerating rare false positives
An ordered set with expected O(log n) search and range scans that's simple to make concurrent

explanation: Two heaps split a stream at its middle, so each median query is O(1) after an O(log n) insert. Union-find answers dynamic connectivity under merges in near-constant amortised time. A Bloom filter trades rare false positives for very little memory. A skip list is a randomised ordered structure with expected O(log n) operations and natural range scans; Redis uses one for sorted sets.
reference: Pugh (1990), Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees

stem: A skip list promotes each node to the next level with probability 1/2. It holds about 1,000,000 keys. About how many levels does it have, and what is the expected search cost?

options.text: About 1,000 levels, and an O(√n) search
options.why: Halving at each level gives logarithmic, not square-root, height.

options.text: About 20 levels, and an expected O(log n) search
options.why: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20, and a search drops about one level per two forward steps.

options.text: Exactly 20 levels, and a worst-case O(log n) search
options.why: The levels are random, so both are expected values; an unlucky run can still be O(n).

options.text: One level, so an O(n) search through a plain sorted list
options.why: The upper levels act as express lanes that skip most of the bottom list.

explanation: With p = 1/2, about n/2^i nodes reach level i, so the top level is near log₂ n ≈ 20 for a million keys. A search starts at the top and moves right until the next key is too large, then drops down a level. That is O(log n) expected, using O(n) expected space. The bounds are probabilistic, unlike AVL or red-black trees, but the structure is simple and suits concurrent implementations.
reference: Pugh (1990), Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees

stem: A Bloom filter has m = 10,000 bits and k = 7 hash functions, and holds n = 1,000 items. Using the estimate (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, roughly what is its false-positive rate?

options.text: About 0.01%
options.why: That would need about 20 bits per item; 10 bits per item gives around 1%.

options.text: About 0.8%
About 7%
options.why: That is roughly the rate with far fewer bits per item, or a badly chosen k.

options.text: About 50%
options.why: About half the bits are set, but a false positive needs all 7 checked bits set: 0.5^7, not 0.5.

explanation: kn/m = 7 × 1,000 / 10,000 = 0.7, and e^(−0.7) ≈ 0.497, so about half of the bits are 1. A false positive needs all k = 7 probed bits set: 0.503^7 ≈ 0.0082, about 0.8%. The optimal k is (m/n) ln 2 ≈ 6.9, so 7 hashes is right here. Ten bits per item giving about 1% is a useful rule of thumb.
reference: Broder & Mitzenmacher (2004), Network Applications of Bloom Filters

stem: Which statements about a binary min-heap with n ≥ 3 distinct elements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Its height is ⌊log₂ n⌋
options.why: It's a complete binary tree, so each level fills before the next starts.

options.text: The second-smallest element is at index 1 or index 2
options.why: It must be a child of the root, because any deeper node has a smaller ancestor besides the root.

options.text: The largest element is always in a leaf
options.why: Any internal node has a larger child, so the maximum can't be internal.

options.text: The largest element is always the last element of the array
options.why: It's in some leaf, but not necessarily the last one; `[1, 9, 2]` is a valid heap.

options.text: Searching for a value takes O(log n) because of the ordering
options.why: The heap property doesn't tell you which subtree to search, so it's O(n).

explanation: A complete tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋; for n = 100 that's 6. The second-smallest has no smaller ancestor except the root, so it must be the root's child at index 1 or 2. The maximum has no larger child, so it is a leaf, and the leaves occupy roughly the second half of the array, though not necessarily the last slot. Heaps give fast access to one extreme only; finding the maximum in a min-heap is O(n), scanning the leaves.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: A running median uses `lo` (a max-heap of the smaller half) and `hi` (a min-heap of the larger half), keeping `len(lo)` equal to `len(hi)` or one more. Put the steps for adding a number in order.

options.text: Push the new number into `lo`
Pop the largest value from `lo` and push it into `hi`
If `hi` now has more elements than `lo`, move the smallest of `hi` back into `lo`
Read the median from the top of `lo`, or the mean of both tops if the sizes are equal

explanation: Pushing into `lo` and then moving its maximum into `hi` guarantees that every value in `lo` is ≤ every value in `hi`. Without that step a large new value could get stuck in the lower half. The rebalance then restores the size rule. Each insert does at most three heap operations, O(log n), and reading the median is O(1).
reference: LeetCode 295: Find Median from Data Stream

stem: In a standard Bloom filter, deleting an item by setting its k bits back to 0 can make the filter wrongly report other, still-present items as absent.

options.text: True
options.why: Other items may share some of those bits; clearing them breaks their guarantee and causes false negatives.

options.text: False
options.why: Bits aren't owned by a single item, so clearing them affects every item that hashes to them.

explanation: The no-false-negatives guarantee relies on bits only ever being set. Clearing bits for a deletion can zero a bit another present item depends on, so that item is now reported absent. Counting Bloom filters keep a small counter per position and decrement on delete. Cuckoo filters support deletion more compactly.
reference: Fan et al. (2000), Summary Cache (counting Bloom filters)

options.why: This is the intended result, but popping from a negated heap removes the largest value, not the smallest.
Negation makes `heappop` remove the largest original value, so the k smallest survive.

options.text: `[3, 7, 8]`, a mix of kept and evicted values
options.why: The pops consistently evict the largest value, so no large value survives.
Besides the wrong values, the result goes through `sorted`, so it would be ascending.

explanation: To keep the k largest, you need a min-heap of size k, so that each pop evicts the smallest kept value. Negating turns the heap into a max-heap of the originals, so every pop evicts the largest value seen. The heap ends up holding the k smallest, giving [1, 2, 3]. Fix: push `x` (not `-x`) and return `sorted(h)`. The negated version is exactly the right tool for the k smallest.
reference: Python docs: heapq.nlargest

stem: A scheduler keeps tasks in a `heapq` and often raises a task's priority. Each change pushes a new `(priority, task_id)` entry and records the latest priority in `current[task_id]`. What must the consumer do when it pops an entry?

options.text: Nothing; heapq automatically drops the older entry for the same task
options.why: heapq has no notion of identity; both entries stay in the heap until popped.

options.text: Call `heapify` after every update so stale entries are removed
options.why: `heapify` restores order but deletes nothing, and it costs O(n) per update.

options.text: Discard it if its priority differs from `current[task_id]`
options.why: Stale copies are discarded lazily when they surface, keeping each update O(log n).

options.text: Run the task only if a second entry for the same task is still in the heap
options.why: That would delay or drop work arbitrarily; the latest recorded priority decides validity.

explanation: This is lazy deletion. Instead of an O(n) search-and-remove, push a fresh entry in O(log n) and discard stale ones when they reach the top: `if prio != current[task_id]: continue`. The heap can hold up to the total number of pushes, so very update-heavy workloads may rebuild it occasionally. Dijkstra's algorithm in Python uses the same pattern with `if d > dist[u]: continue`.
reference: Python docs: heapq — Priority Queue Implementation Notes

stem: A union-find uses union by size (the smaller tree goes under the larger) but no path compression. What is the worst-case cost of a single `find` on n elements?

options.why: Trees can still have several levels; only full compression after the fact flattens them.

options.text: O(α(n)) worst case
options.why: α(n) is an amortised bound that needs path compression as well; it doesn't bound a single find here.

options.text: O(log n)
options.why: A node's depth rises only when its tree at least doubles in size, which can happen at most log₂ n times.

options.text: O(n)
options.why: That is the chain worst case of naive linking, which union by size prevents.

explanation: When a node's tree is attached under a tree at least as large, the node's depth grows by 1 and its new tree is at least twice as big. Sizes can double at most log₂ n times, so depth stays at most log₂ n. Adding path compression brings the amortised cost down to O(α(n)). Naive linking, as in DSA-HEA-022, can build an O(n) chain.
reference: CLRS, Section 21.3: Disjoint-set forests

stem: Which statements about choosing between `heapq.nlargest(k, data)`, `max(data)` and `sorted(data, reverse=True)[:k]` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: For k = 1, `max(data)` is simpler and faster than `nlargest(1, data)`
options.why: The heapq docs recommend `min()`/`max()` for a single item: one O(n) pass with no heap.

options.text: When k approaches n, sorting is usually faster than `nlargest`
options.why: The docs note that for larger k, `sorted()` is more efficient, because O(n log k) gains nothing when k ≈ n.

options.text: `nlargest` always beats sorting, whatever k is
options.why: Its advantage shrinks as k grows; at k close to n, the heap's overhead loses to Timsort.

options.text: `nlargest` returns its results in arbitrary order
options.why: It returns a list sorted from largest to smallest.

options.text: `nlargest` needs O(n) extra memory for the whole input
options.why: It keeps a heap of only k items, O(k) memory, so it works on long iterators.

explanation: The heapq docs say: `nlargest` and `nsmallest` perform best for smaller k; for larger k, `sorted()` is more efficient, and for k = 1, `min()` and `max()` are. `nlargest` costs O(n log k) time and O(k) memory and returns results in descending order. In interviews, saying why you pick each tool scores better than always reaching for a heap.
reference: Python docs: heapq.nlargest

options.why: That is the correct output, but the code never moves values from `hi` back to `lo`.
Every later value goes into `hi`, `lo` stays [1], and the tops 1 and 2 are averaged each time.
`lo` keeps only 1, so its top never reaches 2 or 3.

options.text: It raises IndexError on the second number
options.why: `lo` is non-empty after the first push, so `-lo[0]` never fails.

explanation: For ascending input, every x > 1 goes into `hi`. The rebalance only handles `lo` being too big, never `hi` being too big, so `lo` stays [1] while `hi` grows to [2, 3, 4, 5]. Each step then computes (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5. Fix: add `elif len(hi) > len(lo): heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))`. Sorted input is the classic test that exposes one-sided rebalancing.
reference: LeetCode 295: Find Median from Data Stream

stem:
What does this print?

```python
p = list(range(5))
def find(x):
    while p[x] != x:
        x = p[x]
    return x
def union(a, b):
    p[a] = b

union(0, 1); union(0, 2); union(3, 4)
print(find(1) == find(2), find(0) == find(1), p)
```

options.why: That assumes the second union linked 1 to 2, but it rewrites p[0] instead.

options.text: `True False [2, 1, 2, 4, 4]`, with only 0 split off
options.why: 1 and 2 are both still their own roots, so `find(1) == find(2)` is False.

options.text: `False False [2, 1, 2, 4, 4]`
options.why: union(0, 2) overwrites p[0] = 1 with p[0] = 2, cutting 0 off from 1.

options.text: `False True [2, 1, 2, 4, 4]`
options.why: find(0) is 2 and find(1) is 1, so 0 and 1 now look disconnected.

explanation: `union` must link roots, `p[find(a)] = find(b)`, not the nodes themselves. Here union(0, 1) sets p[0] = 1, then union(0, 2) overwrites it with p[0] = 2, so the earlier merge is lost. Afterwards 1 and 2 are separate roots, and 0 hangs under 2. The code calls union(0, 1) and union(0, 2), so the correct answer would be True True. Linking nodes instead of roots is the most common union-find bug in interviews.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 21: Data Structures for Disjoint Sets

stem: A binary heap holds 100 elements. What is the height of the tree, counting edges on the longest root-to-leaf path? Type a number.
explanation: A complete binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋. 2^6 = 64 ≤ 100 < 128 = 2^7, so the height is 6. Levels 0 to 5 hold 63 nodes and level 6 holds the remaining 37. A push or pop on this heap does at most 6 swaps.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 6: Heapsort

stem: You merge k sorted files lazily, each far too large for memory, keeping one cursor per file in a heap. What extra memory does the merge need, ignoring the output?

options.text: O(N), where N is the total number of records
options.why: The merge streams the records and never holds them all at once.

options.text: O(k): one heap entry per file
options.why: Only the current head record of each file sits in the heap at any moment.

options.text: O(N log k), the same as the running time
options.why: This mixes up time and space; the log factor is time spent per heap operation.

options.text: O(1), because merging needs no extra space
options.why: Picking the minimum across k files needs to know the k current candidates.

explanation: A k-way merge holds one candidate per input in a min-heap: O(k) memory, O(N log k) time. That's why external sorting merges sorted runs this way, and why `heapq.merge(*files)` returns a lazy iterator. Include a source index in each heap entry, `(value, file_idx)`, so you know which file to read next and ties never compare file objects.
reference: Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, Section 5.4.1: Multiway merging

stem: Which statements comparing a skip list with a balanced binary search tree (such as a red-black tree) are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The skip list's O(log n) bounds are expected, not worst case
options.why: Node levels come from coin flips, so an unlucky sequence can produce long searches.

options.text: Skip lists are often easier to make concurrent
options.why: Updates touch a few local pointers with no rotations, which suits lock-free designs.

options.text: Skip lists guarantee O(log n) worst-case search, like red-black trees
options.why: Only the expected cost is logarithmic; the worst case is O(n).

options.text: Skip lists can't support range queries
options.why: The bottom level is a sorted linked list, so range scans are natural.

options.text: Skip lists always use less memory than a sorted array
options.why: Each node carries extra forward pointers, about 2 per node on average with p = 1/2.

explanation: Skip lists trade deterministic bounds for simplicity. Search, insert and delete are O(log n) expected, with no rebalancing rotations, and range scans walk the bottom list. Java's `ConcurrentSkipListMap` exploits the easy concurrency. Redis sorted sets combine a skip list, for ordered ranges, with a hash table, for O(1) score lookup. Balanced BSTs give guaranteed O(log n) but have more complex code.
reference: Pugh (1990), Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees

stem: An old database uses ISAM (indexed sequential access method): a static multi-level index built once, with new records placed in overflow chains. Why does performance degrade on an insert-heavy table, compared with a B+ tree?

options.text: ISAM rebuilds its whole index on every insert
options.why: It's the opposite: the index is static and isn't updated as records arrive.

options.text: Overflow chains grow while the static index never splits
options.why: B+ trees split and rebalance nodes, keeping every lookup at a fixed height.

options.text: ISAM keeps records unsorted, so every lookup is a full scan
options.why: The primary data pages are sorted and indexed; only the overflow records sit outside that order.

options.text: ISAM can only index integer keys
options.why: ISAM can index any key type that has an ordering.

explanation: ISAM builds a sorted index once. Later inserts that don't fit their page go into overflow chains, which the index doesn't describe. As chains grow, lookups and range scans follow more pointers until a periodic reorganisation rebuilds the file. B+ trees split full nodes on insert and stay balanced, so lookups remain O(log n) with no reorganisation. That is why they replaced ISAM in most databases, and why ISAM still suits mostly read-only data.
reference: Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, Database Management Systems, Chapter 10

options.text: Both return `[4, 7, 9]`, since the two calls are interchangeable
options.why: `heapreplace` always inserts x, even when x is smaller than everything kept.

options.text: `a` returns `[2, 7, 9]` and `b` returns `[4, 7, 9]`
options.why: `a` evicts 4 for 1, then 1 for 2; `b` rejects 1 and 2 because each is smaller than the root.

options.text: `a` returns `[4, 7, 9]` and `b` returns `[2, 7, 9]`
options.why: This swaps the two functions' behaviour.

options.text: Both return `[1, 2, 9]`
options.why: Neither ever evicts 9, and `b` keeps 4 and 7.

explanation: Start with heap [4, 7, 9]. `heapreplace(h, 1)` pops 4 and pushes 1 unconditionally, giving [1, 7, 9]; then 2 replaces 1, giving [2, 7, 9]. That's wrong for a top-k. `heappushpop(h, x)` pushes then pops, so a small x comes straight back out and the heap keeps [4, 7, 9]. Use `heappushpop`, or check `if x > h[0]` before `heapreplace`.
reference: Python docs: heapq.heappushpop, heapq.heapreplace

stem: A union-find uses both path compression and union by rank. Which statements about its cost are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Any sequence of m operations on n elements costs O(m α(n))
options.why: This is the Tarjan bound, where α is the inverse Ackermann function.

options.text: α(n) is at most 4 for any input size you'd ever meet
options.why: α grows so slowly that it stays ≤ 4 for n far beyond the number of atoms in the universe.

options.text: Each individual operation is guaranteed O(1) in the worst case
options.why: The bound is amortised; one find can still walk a path of length O(log n).

options.text: The bound is O(m log* n) and can't be improved
options.why: log* n is an older, looser bound; Tarjan proved the tighter α(n) and showed it optimal.

options.text: Rank stays exactly equal to tree height after compression
options.why: Compression lowers heights without updating ranks, so rank becomes only an upper bound.

explanation: Tarjan (1975) proved that with both heuristics, m operations take O(m α(n)) time, and that this is optimal for pointer-machine algorithms. Because α(n) ≤ 4 for any practical n, union-find is effectively linear overall. The guarantee is amortised, though, so one expensive find can occur. Ranks are left alone after compression and serve only as upper bounds on height.
reference: Tarjan (1975), Efficiency of a Good But Not Linear Set Union Algorithm
